source: The Field of a Charged Rod
Add up dE = k dq/r² as components to find the field of a charged rod.
Students add the sizes of the pieces dE without splitting them into components, or miss the components that cancel by symmetry.

You know how to add the fields of several point charges: find each one's field at the point, then add them as vectors. A charged rod is the same problem with infinitely many charges. Cut it into pieces $dq = \lambda\,dx$ (charge densities), treat each piece as a point charge, and add the pieces with an integral.

Each piece makes $dE = \dfrac{k\,dq}{r^2}$, pointing away from the piece (for positive charge). Split it into components and integrate each one separately:
        $$E_x = \int dE_x, \qquad E_y = \int dE_y.$$
        Use symmetry first: components that cancel in mirror-image pairs integrate to zero.

An integral adds numbers, not arrows. Two arrows of size 3 at right angles add to 4.2, not 6. So we turn one vector sum into two ordinary sums, one per component, where plain addition is correct. The size $dE$ may be added directly only when every piece's field points the same way, as for a point on the rod's own line.

A $10\ \text{nC}$ rod $40\ \text{cm}$ long, with P $10\ \text{cm}$ above its middle. With more pieces the vector sum settles on the exact integral, $4020\ \text{N/C}$; adding the sizes stays about 24% too high.
A recipe for any shape
Worked examples
A rod $0.20\ \text{m}$ long carries $8.0\ \text{nC}$ spread evenly. Find the field at a point on the rod's line, $0.10\ \text{m}$ beyond one end.
On the rod's own line
$E \approx 2400\ \text{N/C}$, along the rod's line, away from the rod
Put P at the origin and the rod from $x = a = 0.10\ \text{m}$ to $x = a + L = 0.30\ \text{m}$. Every piece pushes along the same line, so here the sizes may be added.
$$E = \int_a^{a+L}\frac{k\lambda\,dx}{x^2} = k\lambda\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{a+L}\right) = \frac{kQ}{a(a+L)}$$ using $\lambda L = Q$.
Check: far away ($a \gg L$) this is $kQ/a^2$, a point charge.
A rod $0.40\ \text{m}$ long carries $10\ \text{nC}$. Find the field $d = 0.10\ \text{m}$ above its midpoint.
Above the middle
$E \approx 4020\ \text{N/C}$
Rod from $x = -L/2$ to $L/2$, P at $(0, d)$. A piece at $x$ is $r = \sqrt{x^2 + d^2}$ away.
Mirror pieces at $\pm x$ cancel each other's $x$-parts. The $y$-part of each is $dE\cos\theta = \dfrac{k\lambda\,dx}{r^2}\cdot\dfrac{d}{r}$.

$$E = k\lambda d\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}\frac{dx}{(x^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$$ With the substitution $x = d\tan\theta$, $dx = d\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$, the integrand becomes $\cos\theta\,d\theta/d^2$, so the antiderivative is $\dfrac{x}{d^2\sqrt{x^2 + d^2}}$.
$$E = \frac{k\lambda L}{d\sqrt{d^2 + L^2/4}} = \frac{kQ}{d\sqrt{d^2 + L^2/4}}$$
$$E = \frac{(8.99 \times 10^{9})(10 \times 10^{-9})}{(0.10)\sqrt{0.010 + 0.040}} = 4020\ \text{N/C}$$ pointing straight away from the rod.
Check the result $E = kQ/\left(d\sqrt{d^2 + L^2/4}\right)$ far away and very close.
Two checks on the answer
Both limits come out right, a good sign the integral is correct.
Far away, $d \gg L$: the square root is about $d$, so $E \approx kQ/d^2$. From far off, the rod looks like a point.
Very close, $d \ll L$: the root is about $L/2$, so $E \approx \dfrac{2kQ}{dL} = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{d}$. Up close, the rod looks endless. Gauss's law will give the same $2k\lambda/d$ in one line.

Adding the sizes $dE$. Integrating $k\lambda\,dx/r^2$ without the factor $d/r$ treats every piece's field as if it pointed straight up. For the second example that gives $\dfrac{2k\lambda}{d}\arctan\dfrac{L}{2d} = 4980\ \text{N/C}$, about 24% too big. The sideways parts point left and right and cancel; only the parts along the bisector survive. Quick check: unless every piece pushes along the same line, the true field is smaller than the sum of the sizes.
At a point that is not on a line of symmetry (above one end of the rod, say), nothing cancels. Then you must integrate both $dE_x$ and $dE_y$, and the field tilts away from the rod.
